title: Give it a real database
goal: Replace the hardcoded list with PostgreSQL. One database container, a versioned schema, and a test that runs against a real Postgres rather than an in-memory imitation.
startWith: Step 01 finished: the app runs and GET /api/v1/accounts returns the hardcoded account. Docker Desktop running.

newIdeas.plain: A numbered SQL file, e.g. V1__baseline.sql, that Flyway runs once and then records in a table called flyway_schema_history. Your schema becomes a sequence of small, reviewable, replayable changes instead of a thing someone changed by hand.

Tells Hibernate: check that the tables match my entities and fail loudly if they do not. The alternative, update, lets Hibernate silently alter your schema — convenient locally and catastrophic in production. Use validate from day one so the two never diverge.

An @Entity is a mutable class Hibernate manages, mirroring a table. Your domain record is an immutable business type. You keep both and map between them, so a schema change does not ripple into your business rules and Hibernate's requirements (no-arg constructor, non-final fields) do not infect them.

A port is an interface your application defines for something it needs, e.g. AccountRepository. An adapter is an implementation of it that knows a specific technology, e.g. a JPA one. The application depends on the interface, so the technology can be swapped or faked in tests.

A library that starts a real Docker container for the duration of your test and throws it away afterwards. You test against actual PostgreSQL — real types, real constraints — instead of H2, which quietly behaves differently.
A Spring Boot annotation on a Testcontainers container that points spring.datasource.* at that container automatically. Without it you hand-wire the JDBC URL with @DynamicPropertySource.

tasks.do: Start a single Postgres 17 container with Docker Compose
tasks.why: You want a database that behaves like the production one, and that you can throw away and recreate in ten seconds.
tasks.how: Create infra/compose/docker-compose.yml one level above the service, so later services share it. The init script creates the databases the later steps need — writing them now saves editing this file five more times. One database per service is a rule this project takes seriously: services never read each other's tables. The named pgdata volume matters: Postgres only creates POSTGRES_USER and runs the init script when the data directory is empty, so if you ever change the credentials or edit the init script you must down -v first. Without a named volume the anonymous one survives and you get role "ledgerflow" does not exist with no obvious cause.

blocks.label: infra/compose/docker-compose.yml — run from inside account-service/
blocks.body:
mkdir -p ../infra/compose && cat > ../infra/compose/docker-compose.yml << 'EOF'
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17
    container_name: lf-postgres
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ledgerflow
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerflow
      POSTGRES_DB: account
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    volumes:
      - "./init-databases.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sh"
      - "pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ledgerflow"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  pgdata:
EOF

blocks.label: infra/compose/init-databases.sh — one database per service, created up front
blocks.body:
cat > ../infra/compose/init-databases.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Runs once, the first time the volume is created.
# account already exists (POSTGRES_DB); these are for later steps.
set -e
for db in ledger notification payment issuer settlement balance risk; do
  psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -c "CREATE DATABASE \"$db\";"
done
EOF
chmod +x ../infra/compose/init-databases.sh

check.expect: A list including account, ledger, payment, issuer, settlement, balance, notification, risk.

tasks.do: Add the JPA, Postgres, Flyway and Testcontainers dependencies
tasks.why: Four libraries, each with one job: talk to the database, drive Postgres, version the schema, and start a throwaway database in tests.
tasks.how: Paste these inside the existing <dependencies> block in pom.xml. No version numbers — the Boot parent supplies them. flyway-database-postgresql is separate from flyway-core and is easy to forget; without it Flyway starts and then refuses to recognise Postgres. Watch the Testcontainers artifactIds: Boot 4 pins Testcontainers 2.0, which renamed every module from postgresql to testcontainers-postgresql. Paste the 1.x name and the BOM has no version for it, so Maven fails the build with 'dependencies.dependency.version' ... is missing before it compiles anything.

tasks.do: Point the app at Postgres and set ddl-auto to validate
tasks.why: Configuration in one file, in a format you will re-use in every service that follows.
tasks.how: Delete the generated application.properties and use YAML instead — nested keys are easier to read once there are twenty of them. open-in-view: false turns off a Spring default that keeps a database session open for the whole HTTP request; leaving it on hides lazy-loading bugs until they hit production.

blocks.label: src/main/resources/application.yml (delete application.properties)
blocks.body:
rm -f src/main/resources/application.properties
cat > src/main/resources/application.yml << 'EOF'
spring:
  application:
    name: account-service
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/account
    username: ledgerflow
    password: ledgerflow
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate      # never 'update'. not even locally.
    open-in-view: false
  flyway:
    enabled: true
EOF

tasks.why: The schema is now code: reviewable, versioned, and identical on every machine.
tasks.how: Flyway looks in src/main/resources/db/migration and runs anything it has not run before, in version order. Never edit a migration that has already run — Flyway stores a checksum and will refuse to start. To change something, add V3__…. The seed data matters: the account id below is the one every curl command in this project uses.

blocks.label: src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__baseline.sql
src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__seed.sql — do this or later steps have nothing to book
blocks.body:
cat > src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__seed.sql << 'EOF'
INSERT INTO accounts (id, name) VALUES
  ('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'Demo Arena');

INSERT INTO wallets (id, account_id, label)
SELECT gen_random_uuid(), '11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'A-' || i
FROM generate_series(1, 20) AS i;
EOF

check.run: docker exec -it lf-postgres psql -U ledgerflow -d account -c 'SELECT version, description, success FROM flyway_schema_history;'
check.expect: Two rows, both success = t. Run the app once first — Flyway applies migrations at startup.

tasks.do: Add JPA entities and a repository under adapter/out/persistence
tasks.why: This is where the database lives. Everything Hibernate needs stays in this folder and nowhere else.
tasks.how: Three files: an entity that mirrors the table, a Spring Data interface, and an adapter that converts entities into your domain records. The entity has a no-arg constructor and mutable fields because Hibernate requires them — which is exactly why you do not want your business types to be entities.

blocks.label: adapter/out/persistence/AccountEntity.java
adapter/out/persistence/WalletEntity.java
adapter/out/persistence/JpaAccountRepository.java — Spring Data writes the implementation
adapter/out/persistence/AccountRepositoryAdapter.java — entity in, domain record out

tasks.do: Define the AccountRepository port and make the controller use it
tasks.why: The controller should ask for accounts without knowing whether they come from Postgres, a cache, or a test double.
tasks.how: The interface lives in application/ — the layer that owns the use cases — and the JPA class in adapter/out/persistence implements it. That direction matters: the application defines what it needs, the adapter satisfies it. Notice your domain records did not change at all when the database arrived.

blocks.label: application/AccountRepository.java — the port
adapter/in/web/AccountController.java — replaces the hardcoded version

check.run:
./mvnw spring-boot:run
# then, in another terminal:
curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts | jq '.[0].wallets | length'
check.expect: 20 — and the wallet ids are now stable across restarts, because they come from the database.

tasks.why: A test that runs against real PostgreSQL catches the things H2 hides: real constraint violations, real types, real SQL.
tasks.how: @ServiceConnection is the piece that makes this short — it wires spring.datasource.* to the container Spring just started. The first run pulls the postgres:17 image and is slow; later runs are quick. Flyway runs inside the container too, so the test exercises your migrations as well as your code.

blocks.label: src/test/java/io/ledgerflow/account/AccountRepositoryIT.java
Run it — the container starts and stops by itself

check.expect: Green. Docker shows a postgres container appearing and disappearing during the run — that is the test's own database, unrelated to your Compose one.

proof.expect: Tests green, app starts clean, /api/v1/accounts serves rows that came out of Postgres.
proof.note: Two databases are in play and that is intentional: Compose runs the one your app uses, Testcontainers starts a separate throwaway one for the tests.

doneWhen: Tests spin up a real Postgres and pass, and the app starts clean against Compose with ddl-auto set to validate.

lessons.title: Database tool window
lessons.teach: Open View → Tool Windows → Database and add your Postgres data source. From then on you inspect tables and run SQL without leaving the IDE — and Flyway migrations get schema-aware completion.
lessons.fallbackTip: Ultimate only. Community: psql inside the container.

lessons.title: New file without leaving the keyboard
lessons.teach: Your first Flyway migration needs an exact name. Select the folder and press Ctrl+Alt+Insert (New → File) rather than reaching for the mouse — and note the IDE will not let you create it twice.
